title: From eigenvalues to the SVD
summary: Symmetric matrices have perpendicular eigenvectors; the eigenvalues of AᵀA are σ², and its unit eigenvectors are the right singular vectors.

blocks.title: A symmetric matrix

define.meaning: $S^\mathsf{T} = S$: the entry in row $i$, column $j$ equals the one in row $j$, column $i$. Its two off-diagonal entries are equal.

blocks.why: Lesson 3's $B$ had eigenvectors at an angle. Lesson 1's matrix is symmetric; see whether that changes things.
blocks.prompt: $S = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$ has eigenvectors $(1, 1)$ for 3 and $(1, -1)$ for 1. Compute $(1, 1) \cdot (1, -1)$.

slips.say: $1 \cdot (-1)$ is $-1$, so the second product cancels the first.

hints: Multiply entry by entry, then add.

check.say: Sketch $y = x$ and $y = -x$: they cross at a right angle.

blocks.solution: 0: perpendicular. This always holds: for a symmetric matrix, eigenvectors with different eigenvalues are perpendicular. The SVD rests on it.

blocks.title: Which has perpendicular eigenvectors?
blocks.why: The rule is about the matrix, so you can tell before finding a single eigenvector.
blocks.prompt: Each of these matrices has two different eigenvalues. Which one is sure to have perpendicular eigenvectors?

options.say: Right. It is symmetric (both off-diagonal entries are 3). Its eigenvectors are $(1, 1)$ and $(1, -1)$, with dot product 0.
Not this one. It is lesson 3's $B$: the off-diagonal entries differ, and its eigenvectors $(1, 1)$ and $(1, -2)$ have dot product $-1$.
Not this one. Not symmetric ($1 \ne 0$). Its eigenvectors are $(1, 0)$ for 2 and $(1, 1)$ for 3, with dot product 1.
Not this one. Not symmetric ($0 \ne 1$). Its eigenvectors are $(1, 1)$ for 3 and $(0, 1)$ for 2, with dot product 1.

blocks.hint: Look for the matrix that equals its own transpose.
blocks.solution: Symmetric means perpendicular eigenvectors. $A^\mathsf{T}A$ is always symmetric, which is why the SVD starts from it.

blocks.title: AᵀA
blocks.why: Any matrix $A$, symmetric or not, gives a symmetric $A^\mathsf{T}A$. Its eigenvalues and eigenvectors are where the SVD of $A$ comes from.

slips.say: That is $AA^\mathsf{T}$: rows dotted with rows. $A^\mathsf{T}A$ dots columns with columns.

hints: Row $i$, column $j$ of $A^\mathsf{T}A$ is (column $i$ of $A$) $\cdot$ (column $j$ of $A$).

check.say: It must be symmetric: top-right equals bottom-left. The diagonal entries are the squared lengths of the columns.

blocks.title: The eigenvalues of AᵀA
blocks.why: These two numbers will be the squares of the stretches of $A$.
blocks.prompt: For $A = \begin{bmatrix}2&2\\-1&1\end{bmatrix}$, $A^\mathsf{T}A = \begin{bmatrix}5&3\\3&5\end{bmatrix}$. Find the eigenvalues of $A^\mathsf{T}A$, largest first.
hints: Two numbers that add to 10 and multiply to 16.

check.say: They add to 10 and multiply to 16. Both should be positive or zero: the eigenvalues of an $A^\mathsf{T}A$ always are.

blocks.solution: 8 and 2. The eigenvectors are $(1, 1)$ and $(1, -1)$, as for $\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$: perpendicular, since $A^\mathsf{T}A$ is symmetric.

blocks.title: v₁, a unit eigenvector

define.meaning: $v_i$, the unit eigenvector of $A^\mathsf{T}A$ for its $i$-th largest eigenvalue. Unit means length 1.

blocks.why: The SVD needs a direction and a length of 1, so that $v_1$ and $v_2$ form a pair of perpendicular unit axes.
blocks.prompt: $A^\mathsf{T}A = \begin{bmatrix}5&3\\3&5\end{bmatrix}$ has largest eigenvalue 8. Find $v_1$, its unit eigenvector for 8.

answer.acceptNote: Either sign is right: $-v_1$ lies on the same line and also has length 1.

slips.say: The right direction. Now make it length 1: divide by its length, $\sqrt{1^2 + 1^2}$.
Divide by the length of $(1, 1)$, which is $\sqrt2$, not 2.

hints: Solve $(A^\mathsf{T}A - 8I)\,v = 0$ for a direction, then scale it to length 1.

check.say: A unit vector has $x^2 + y^2 = 1$. And $A^\mathsf{T}A$ times it should be 8 times it.

blocks.solution: $v_1 = (1, 1)/\sqrt2$. In the same way $v_2 = (1, -1)/\sqrt2$, perpendicular to it.

blocks.title: The singular values
blocks.why: $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ are the stretches in the rotate, stretch, rotate picture of $A$. They come straight from eigenvalues.
blocks.prompt: $A = \begin{bmatrix}2&2\\-1&1\end{bmatrix}$, and $A^\mathsf{T}A$ has eigenvalues 8 and 2. Find $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$. Type a square root as sqrt( ).

slips.say: Those are the eigenvalues $\lambda$ of $A^\mathsf{T}A$. Each $\sigma$ is the square root of one.
That halves the eigenvalues. A singular value is the square root: $\sigma = \sqrt{\lambda}$.

hints: Take the square root of each eigenvalue, largest first.
blocks.solution: $\sigma_1 = 2\sqrt2$ and $\sigma_2 = \sqrt2$. With $v_1, v_2$ from the eigenvectors, that is the stretch half of the SVD, all from eigenvalues.

blocks.title: A times (1, 1)
blocks.why: A singular value is a stretch. Send $v_1$'s direction through $A$ and watch the length change.

slips.say: That is $A^\mathsf{T}(1, 1)$: you used the columns of $A$ as rows. Row 1 of $A$ is $(2, 2)$.

hints: Each entry is a row of $A$ dotted with $(1, 1)$, which adds up that row.

check.say: Its squared length should be $\lambda_1 = 8$ times the squared length of $(1, 1)$, which is 2.

blocks.solution: $(4, 0)$ has length 4; $(1, 1)$ has length $\sqrt2$. So $A$ stretches this direction by $4/\sqrt2 = 2\sqrt2 = \sigma_1$. Note $(4, 0)$ is not along $(1, 1)$: $A$ also turns it. $v_1$ is not an eigenvector of $A$, only of $A^\mathsf{T}A$.

blocks.title: The stretch along (1, −1)
blocks.why: The second right singular vector should be stretched by $\sigma_2$. Check it with lengths alone.
blocks.prompt: With $A = \begin{bmatrix}2&2\\-1&1\end{bmatrix}$: by what factor does $A$ stretch $(1, -1)$? That is, find $\|A\,(1, -1)\| \,/\, \|(1, -1)\|$.

slips.say: That is the length of $A\,(1, -1)$. Divide by the length of $(1, -1)$ too.
Compare lengths, not the vectors' entries. What is the length of $A\,(1, -1)$?

check.say: It should equal $\sigma_2$ from two screens back: the square root of $A^\mathsf{T}A$'s smaller eigenvalue.

blocks.solution: $2/\sqrt2 = \sqrt2 = \sigma_2$. And $(4, 0)$ and $(0, -2)$ are perpendicular: the left singular vectors $u_1, u_2$ point along them. Every piece of the SVD of $A$ came from an eigenvalue problem you can now do by hand.
